content.body:
### Summary

The `plugin-manager add` command uses the `name` field from the plugin manifest directly as a filename when writing the downloaded binary to disk, without any sanitization or validation. This enables two attack vectors:

1. **Plugin Override** — A malicious plugin repository can set the manifest `name` to match an existing plugin (e.g. `OpenShiftPlugin`), silently overwriting it with a trojanized version. The trojanized plugin can perform all legitimate transformations while injecting rogue Kubernetes resources into the transform output, which the user then unknowingly applies to their cluster.

2. **Path Traversal** — The manifest `name` can contain `../../` sequences, allowing the attacker to write an executable file (with 0777 permissions) to any location the user has write access to. This is significantly worse if crane is run with `sudo`, as it could overwrite system binaries.

### Root Cause

In [`cmd/plugin-manager/add/add.go` line 232](https://github.com/migtools/crane/blob/main/cmd/plugin-manager/add/add.go#L232):

```go
pluginBinary, err := os.OpenFile(filepath+"/"+filename, syscall.O_RDWR|syscall.O_CREAT|syscall.O_TRUNC, 0777)
```

The `filename` parameter comes from `value.Name` in the plugin manifest YAML. There is no validation that:
- The name matches what the user actually requested to install
- The name does not contain path traversal characters (`/`, `\`, `..`)

Additionally, the `Validate` step in `add.go` only checks if the user-provided name (e.g. `CoolPlugin`) already exists in the plugins directory — it does not check the actual `name` from the manifest (e.g. `OpenShiftPlugin`), so the overwrite is not detected.

### Proof of Concept

A full end-to-end PoC is available at: https://github.com/RanWurmbrand/compromised-plugins

content.body:
###  Description
 When installing a plugin via crane plugin-manager add, the plugin binary is created with mode 0777 and the plugin directory with os.ModePerm (0777):
https://github.com/konveyor/crane/blob/main/cmd/plugin-manager/add/add.go#L225-L232

### Risk

The plugin binary and its directory are created with 0777 permissions. If the system's umask doesn't strip the extra bits, every user on the machine can overwrite the plugin file. An attacker can replace it with malicious code, and the next time someone runs crane, it executes that code with their permissions — including access to their Kubernetes clusters and credentials.

This is worse for --global installs (/usr/local/share/crane/plugins), where all users on the machine share the same plugin directory - one compromised plugin affects everyone.

## Note 
In practice, most systems have a default umask (022) that strips the dangerous bits automatically, so most users are protected. But the code should set safe permissions itself rather than relying on the system to fix it.


## Proposed fix:
Use 0755 for both the file mode in os.OpenFile and the directory mode in os.MkdirAll.

**Detected by gosec as G302 (CWE-276).**

content.body:
## Problem
Cross-platform OpenShift e2e runs can fail when source and target clusters use different StorageClass names. For example, an AWS source may default to `gp3-csi`, while a GCP target exposes `standard-csi` and `ssd-csi`. `transfer-pvc` copies the source PVC spec unless `--dest-storage-class` is supplied, and applying rendered manifests can then attempt an immutable StorageClass change.

## Observed impact
The target PVC can remain Pending with an event such as `storageclass.storage.k8s.io "gp3-csi" not found`. Tests may also fail later when applying a rendered PVC manifest that still contains the source StorageClass.

## Scope
Make cross-cluster PVC-transfer e2e tests resolve the target default StorageClass dynamically, pass it to `transfer-pvc`, and pass a source-to-target `pvc-storage-class-map` when rendered PVC manifests are applied. Same-platform migrations must continue to work when source and target defaults have the same name. Do not change the CLI's intentional source-spec behavior without a separate product decision.

## Acceptance criteria
- Tier1 and tier0 cross-cluster PVC-transfer tests work across AWS, GCP, and same-platform OpenShift clusters.
- Destination PVCs use a valid target StorageClass.
- Rendered PVC manifests do not attempt to change an existing PVC to an incompatible or immutable source StorageClass.
- Tests retain their original behavioral assertions and clean up namespaces/resources.

## Child issues
- [ ] https://github.com/migtools/crane/issues/1011
- [ ] https://github.com/migtools/crane/issues/1012

content.body:
## Summary
The Crane E2E workflows can fail because Ginkgo's default suite timeout is approximately 1 hour, even though the GitHub Actions jobs allow longer runtimes.

## Evidence
Run: https://github.com/migtools/crane/actions/runs/33854000225
PR with the timeout configuration fix: https://github.com/migtools/crane/pull/921

The run failed on both attempts at the Ginkgo suite timeout:

- Attempt 1: `MTA-804` timed out during deferred cleanup while waiting for `kubectl delete namespace ... --wait=true` on the target cluster.
- Attempt 2: `MTA-851` reached the one-hour suite limit while running the final E2E test. The test operations completed, but Ginkgo terminated the suite before completion was reported.

Both attempts ran 34 tests successfully and then ended with `Suite Timeout Elapsed`, while the GitHub job limit was 90 minutes.

## Impact
The E2E workflow reports failures even when the affected test functionality passes. A slow namespace cleanup or cumulative serial test runtime can consume the Ginkgo suite budget and fail otherwise unrelated tests.

## Fix
Increase the GitHub Actions job timeout to 120 minutes and explicitly set the Ginkgo suite timeout to 90 minutes across all E2E execution paths. See PR #921.

Related: #774

content.body:
## Summary

Update `.github/workflows/pr-ready-for-review-slack.yml` so that commenting `/rfr` (or `/ready-for-review`) again can send another Slack notification, without requiring authors to manually remove the `ready-for-review-notified` label or run `/rfr-reset` / `/ready-for-review-reset` first.

## Current behavior

After a successful `/rfr` notification, the workflow adds the `ready-for-review-notified` label. Subsequent `/rfr` comments are skipped while that label is present:

```
PR #N already has ready-for-review-notified label; skipping duplicate notification.
```

Today, re-notifying requires either:
1. Manually removing the `ready-for-review-notified` label, or
2. Running `/rfr-reset` (or `/ready-for-review-reset`) before `/rfr` again

## Desired behavior

When the PR author comments `/rfr` (or `/ready-for-review`) again on an open, non-draft PR, the workflow should send a Slack notification again—even if `ready-for-review-notified` is already present.

## Proposed approach

Update the guard logic in `.github/workflows/pr-ready-for-review-slack.yml` so a fresh `/rfr` is treated as an intentional re-notify rather than a duplicate to skip. Options to consider:

1. **Allow re-notify on every `/rfr`** — remove (or bypass) the `ready-for-review-notified` skip when `/rfr` is posted again.
2. **Auto-reset on `/rfr`** — if the label exists, remove it and proceed with notification (effectively combining `/rfr-reset` + `/rfr`).
3. Keep `/rfr-reset` for explicit reset if still useful, or deprecate it if no longer needed.

Also clarify whether the `ready-for-review-notified` label should still be retained (e.g. for auditing) or if another mechanism is preferred.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Author can comment `/rfr` multiple times and receive Slack notifications each time (for open, non-draft PRs)
- [ ] No manual label removal required between notifications
- [ ] `/rfr-reset` behavior is either updated, documented, or removed if obsolete
- [ ] Non-author comments and draft/closed PRs continue to be ignored as today
- [ ] Workflow still reacts (`+1`) to valid author commands

## References

- Workflow: `.github/workflows/pr-ready-for-review-slack.yml`

content.body:
## Description

After `export → transform → apply`, the generated `output/output.yaml` is intentionally missing **PVCs** for a stateful app. `crane transform` whiteouts `PersistentVolumeClaim` (see crane-lib `gksToWhiteout`), because PV *data* is migrated by `crane transfer-pvc`, which creates the destination PVC itself.

This works OK for current most often scenario migrating from one live cluster to another using export/transform/apply pipeline together with `transfer-pvc` commands. However, e.g. for gitops use-cases missing PVCs cause the application manifests to be incomplete/broken.

## Suggestion 1

1. **un-whiteout PVC** in KubernetesPlugin
2. add check https://github.com/migtools/crane/issues/905

## Suggestion 2

Document the stateful migration workflow explicitly (README / transfer-pvc docs):

1. **`output.yaml` is not self-contained for stateful apps** — the PVCs are whiteouted on purpose and must be created via `transfer-pvc`.
2. **Ordering** — provision + populate the target PVCs with `transfer-pvc` *before* applying `output.yaml`, so the Deployments can bind them.

## Environment

- crane v0.11.0-alpha.1

## Failure

Jenkins job [mta-ops-cli-tests-runner migtools/crane#90](https://jenkins-csb-migrationqe-main.dno.corp.redhat.com/job/mta/job/mta-ops-cli-tests-runner/90/console) fails in the Tier1 suite on OCP.

Failing test: `MTA-899` in `e2e-tests/tests/tier1/mta_899_openshift_plugin_image_warnings_test.go`

Observed error:

```
unknown command "plugin-manager" for "mta-ops"
```

The suite reports `0 passed, 1 failed, 56 skipped`, and Jenkins exits with code 1. Cluster setup and application deployment complete successfully.

## Cause

The test invokes:

```go
config.CraneBin, "plugin-manager", "add", "OpenShiftPlugin", "--plugin-dir", pluginDir
```

The MTA 8.3.0 binary used by the job (`crane` SHA `198c8853ea36739125b5977d2bb468ec787173b4`) no longer exposes the `plugin-manager` command. `OpenShiftPlugin` is shipped with the binary distribution and should be discovered from the packaged plugin location by `transform`.

## Suggested fix

Update MTA-899 to stop installing `OpenShiftPlugin` with `plugin-manager`. Run `mta-ops transform` without the temporary `--plugin-dir`, allowing the packaged plugin to be discovered. Optionally verify first with `mta-ops transform listplugins` that `OpenShiftPlugin` is available.

The test should continue asserting the expected `ImageStream` warning.

content.body:
## Summary

`crane transform --instructions-file` cannot complete an instructions file
that contains **more than one stage** and **at least one `optionals`** map. The command
runs instruction stages one at a time, but validates the complete map of
per-stage optionals against only the stage currently being run.

## Environment

- `crane version`:

  ```text
  crane:
      Version: main
      SHA: main
  crane-lib:
      Version: v0.0.10
  kustomize:
      Version: v5.8.1
  ```

- Built-in plugins reported by `crane transform list-plugins`:
  `KubernetesPlugin`, `OpenShiftPlugin`, `BuildConfigPlugin`.
- Tested against the WordPress workload in namespace
  `wordpress-instructions-demo` on OpenShift Local (CRC).

## Reproducer

Run crane transform with instructions file:

```yaml
stages:
  - name: KubernetesPlugin
    optionals:
      add-annotations: "migrated-by=crane,migration-demo=multi-stage-optionals"
      strip-default-rbac: "true"
  - name: OpenShiftPlugin
    optionals:
      strip-default-rbac: "true"
      strip-default-cabundle: "true"
```

## Actual Result

The first stage fails because `OpenShiftPlugin` is not part of the selector for
the currently running `KubernetesPlugin` stage:

```text
Invalid stage optional flags: per-stage optionals reference unknown stage "OpenShiftPlugin" (known stages: KubernetesPlugin)
```

Keeping optionals only on `KubernetesPlugin` does not work around the problem.
`KubernetesPlugin` completes, but the next `CustomEdits` stage fails with:

```text
Invalid stage optional flags: per-stage optionals reference unknown stage "KubernetesPlugin" (known stages: CustomEdits)
```

## Expected Result

Each stage should receive only its own `optionals` map. A multi-stage
instructions file with optionals for `KubernetesPlugin`, `OpenShiftPlugin`, and
`BuildConfigPlugin` should run all stages in declared order.

## Impact

The instructions-file schema advertises per-stage optionals, but they cannot be
used in any multi-stage pipeline. The runnable `instructions.yaml` sample is
therefore intentionally option-free.

## Suggested Fix

When executing each instruction stage, pass only the optional values keyed by
that stage to the orchestrator, or validate `StageOptionalFlags` against the
complete instructions stage list rather than the one-stage selector.
content.title: Transform instructions-file fails with per-stage optionals

content.body:
## Description

`crane export` excludes `Event` by default **only when no GK filters are given** (`cmd/export/export.go`):

```go
// Apply default --exclude-gk Event if no GK filters specified
if len(o.includeGK) == 0 && len(o.excludeGK) == 0 {
    o.excludeGK = []string{"Event"}
}
```

As soon as a user passes any `--include-gk` or `--exclude-gk <other-kind>`, this default is **replaced** and `Event` resources are exported.

`KubernetesTransformPlugin` does not whiteout `Event` either — `gksToWhiteout` (crane-lib `transform/kubernetes/kubernetes.go`) lists Endpoints / EndpointSlice / PVC / OLM lifecycle kinds, **but not Event**. So once Events are exported they pass through `transform` and land in `output/output.yaml` as active resources — runtime noise that should not be recreated on the target.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `crane export -n <ns> --exclude-gk Secret` (any custom GK filter, so the default `Event` exclusion is dropped).
2. Events appear under `export/resources/<ns>/...`.
3. `crane transform` + `apply` → the Events survive into `output/output.yaml` (not whiteouted).

## Suggestion (either)

- **Always** exclude `Event` at export regardless of other filters — merge the default with the user-supplied filters instead of replacing them; **or**
- Add `Event` (`{Group: "", Kind: "Event"}` and `events.k8s.io/Event`) to the plugin's default `gksToWhiteout`, so `transform` drops it even if `export` lets it through.

Current workaround: `crane transform --optional-flags extra-whiteouts=Event`.

## Environment

- crane v0.11.0-alpha.1
- crane-lib @ b8fa732 (`transform/kubernetes`)

This is a higher level issue to track this effort. It makes sense to update at least crane-lib part soon to be ready for test day to fully utilize multistage transformation with non-trivial plugins.

Goal: Enable Crane plugins to generate new Kubernetes resources (not just transform existing ones). 

## Context and Motivation

### Current State
The Crane plugin system allows plugins to only:

Transform existing resources using JSONPatch operations
Mark resources for deletion using the whiteout flag
Limitation: Cannot create new resource types that didn't exist in the input data.

### Requirement
Enable plugins to generate new resources for scenarios like:


BuildConfig → Shipwright Build - OpenShift to Kubernetes-native conversion
DeploymentConfig → Deployment - deprecated resource migration
ImageStream → container registry references - OpenShift dependency resolution

### Architecture
```
Input Resources
    ↓
[Orchestrator] → [Runner] → [Plugin]
    ↓                           ↓
RunnerResponse.NewResources ←─┘
    ↓
TransformArtifacts (original + new)
    ↓
[Writer] → Kustomize structure
```

Key Insight: The existing Writer already handles artifacts uniformly, no changes needed!

Details on https://github.com/aufi/move-crane/blob/main/drafts/plugin-update-new-resource-plan.md

content.body:
We need to update the Jenkins pipeline to pass the `--cloud-storage` flag, and update the crane test infra to accept that flag and run the tests as admin.

This is needed to support testing the upcoming indirect data migration (S3/cloud-storage) enhancement, once that lands in crane (currently just a proposal, nothing implemented yet).

Some notes on how this could work, so whoever picks this up has context.

On the crane side, once the enhancement is implemented, transfer-pvc will get new flags like --cloud-storage and --rclone-config-secret that swap the transfer engine from rsync/stunnel to rclone. On the test infra side, all PVC transfers in the e2e suite go through a single function, TransferPVC() in e2e-tests/framework/crane.go, which builds the transfer-pvc command from a TransferPVCOptions struct. That function is the only place any test invokes transfer-pvc, so it's the natural place to make this change.

Rather than updating every individual test to opt into indirect mode, it would be cleaner to have TransferPVC() itself check an environment variable at the start of the function and append the cloud-storage flags when it's set. That way, none of the existing tests need to change at all. Flipping the Jenkins toggle sets the env var, and every test that already calls TransferPVC() transparently runs through indirect mode instead of direct mode.

So on the Jenkins side, this really just needs one boolean parameter that gets threaded into that env var before the test suite runs.

## Summary
`[MTA-801] Migrate all of PVCs that are associated with quiesced resource` (tier0, pvc-transfer) failed during the "Compare YAML semantic diff of golden and actual export files" step for the `redis` app.

**Test:** `crane/e2e-tests/tests/tier0/mta_801_stateful_migration_test.go:69`
**Jenkins run:** https://jenkins-csb-migrationqe-main.dno.corp.redhat.com/job/mta/job/crane-ocp-tests-runner/350/testReport/

## Failure details
The exported resource set does not match the golden file. The actual export contains extra resources that the golden file doesn't expect:

- RoleBindings: `system:deployers`, `system:image-builders`, `system:image-pullers` (present in both `authorization.openshift.io/v1` and `rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1`)
- ServiceAccounts: `builder`, `deployer` (golden only expects `default`)
- Secrets: `dockercfg:builder`, `dockercfg:default`, `dockercfg:deployer`
- ConfigMap: `openshift-service-ca.crt`

```
resource identity sets differ between golden and got directories:
[apps/v1|Deployment|redis|redis apps/v1|ReplicaSet|redis|owner:redis discovery.k8s.io/v1|EndpointSlice|redis|service:redis v1|ConfigMap|redis|kube-root-ca.crt v1|Endpoints|redis|redis v1|PersistentVolumeClaim|redis|redis-data v1|Secret|redis|redis v1|ServiceAccount|redis|default v1|Service|redis|redis]
vs
[apps/v1|Deployment|redis|redis apps/v1|ReplicaSet|redis|owner:redis authorization.openshift.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:deployers authorization.openshift.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:image-builders authorization.openshift.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:image-pullers discovery.k8s.io/v1|EndpointSlice|redis|service:redis rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:deployers rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:image-builders rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1|RoleBinding|redis|system:image-pullers v1|ConfigMap|redis|kube-root-ca.crt v1|ConfigMap|redis|openshift-service-ca.crt v1|Endpoints|redis|redis v1|PersistentVolumeClaim|redis|redis-data v1|Secret|redis|dockercfg:builder v1|Secret|redis|dockercfg:default v1|Secret|redis|dockercfg:deployer v1|Secret|redis|redis v1|ServiceAccount|redis|builder v1|ServiceAccount|redis|default v1|ServiceAccount|redis|deployer v1|Service|redis|redis]
```

## Suggested fix
These extra objects (builder/deployer/image-puller RoleBindings, ServiceAccounts, and their dockercfg Secrets, plus `openshift-service-ca.crt`) are OpenShift's own auto-provisioned per-namespace objects, not resources the user created. Two options:
1. If crane's default export scope is expected to skip these auto-generated objects, update crane's default ignore/skip-resource list to filter them out at export time (they'd be regenerated by OpenShift on the target namespace anyway).
2. If the test cluster's default behavior changed (e.g. newer OpenShift version injects `openshift-service-ca.crt` and additional RBAC bindings by default), update the golden fixture file for this test to include the newly expected objects.

Recommend checking whether other tier0 golden-file tests exhibit the same drift — if so, this is likely an OpenShift version upgrade on the test cluster (`migqe-*`) rather than a one-off, and the fix should be applied consistently (ignore-list vs. golden update) across all affected goldens.

content.body:
## Summary

  `transfer-pvc` fails with an Ingress hostname validation error when the namespace name is long (up to 63 chars, the Kubernetes maximum).

  ## Steps to Reproduce

  ```bash
  # Create namespace at max length (63 chars)
  kubectl create namespace this-is-a-namespace-name-that-is-exactly-sixty-three-chars-long

  # Deploy app with PVC in that namespace
  # ... deploy deployment + PVC ...

  # Transfer PVC using nginx-ingress endpoint
  crane transfer-pvc \
    --source-context src --destination-context tgt \
    --pvc-name data-pvc \
    --pvc-namespace this-is-a-namespace-name-that-is-exactly-sixty-three-chars-long \
    --endpoint nginx-ingress --ingress-class nginx \
    --subdomain "test.172.19.0.2.nip.io"
```

##  Error

  Ingress.networking.k8s.io "data-pvc" is invalid: spec.rules[0].host: Invalid value:
  "data-pvc-this-is-a-namespace-name-that-is-exactly-sixty-three-.e13.172.19.0.2.nip.io":
  a lowercase RFC 1123 subdomain must consist of lower case alphanumeric characters, '-' or '.',
  and must start and end with an alphanumeric character

## Root Cause

  The pvc-transfer library's ingress endpoint constructs the hostname as <pvcName>-<namespace>.<subdomain>. When the combined <pvcName>-<namespace> exceeds 63 chars (DNS label limit), it gets truncated. If the truncation
  lands on a hyphen, the resulting label ends with -, violating RFC 1123.

  In this case:
  - PVC name: data-pvc (8 chars)
  - Namespace: this-is-a-namespace-name-that-is-exactly-sixty-three-chars-long (63 chars)
  - Combined: data-pvc-this-is-a-namespace-name-that-is-exactly-sixty-three- — ends with -

  ## Comparison with Route Endpoint

  The Route endpoint path had the same issue, which was fixed in #625 using truncateWithHash() — it truncates to 53 chars and appends an 8-char MD5 hash suffix, ensuring the label always ends with an alphanumeric
  character. The Ingress endpoint path does not have this fix.

 ## Expected Behavior

  The Ingress hostname should be truncated safely, similar to the Route fix — either by stripping trailing hyphens after truncation or by using the same truncateWithHash() approach.

content.body:
# Issue Proposal Summary

Add a release verification check (script / CI step) that takes a built `crane` or downstream binary built from mta-crane repo, runs its `version` subcommand, extracts the embedded build commit SHA, and verifies that this SHA exists in the expected upstream/downstream branch. The check reports a clear status:

- **GREEN** — the SHA is the latest (HEAD) commit on the expected branch
- **YELLOW** — the SHA exists in the expected branch history, but is not the latest commit
- **RED** — the SHA is not found in the expected branch at all

## Motivation

During the release process, `crane` (upstream) and the downstream, built from `migtools/mta-crane` binaries are produced from specific branches (`release-0.10`, `mta-8.2`, etc.). Today there is no automated way to verify that a shipped binary was actually built from the correct branch and the expected commit. This gap can lead to:

- Shipping a binary built from a stale commit (missing cherry-picked bugfixes)
- Shipping a binary accidentally built from the wrong branch (e.g. `main` instead of `release-0.10`)
- Delayed detection of sync issues between upstream and downstream repos

## How it works

### Version output (existing)

The `version` subcommand already prints the build commit SHA, injected at build time via `-ldflags`:

```
$ crane version
crane:
	Version: v0.10.0
	SHA: b6e8a70...
crane-lib:
	Version: ...
kustomize:
	Version: ...
```

### Proposed check

The check accepts:
1. **Binary path** (or the version output directly via stdin/pipe)
2. **Expected branch mapping** as a parameter, e.g. `--repo=migtools/crane --branch=release-0.10` or `--repo=migtools/mta-crane --branch=mta-8.2`

Steps:
1. Run `<binary> version` and parse the `SHA:` line
2. Query the expected repository+branch to check if the SHA exists in its history (using `git branch --contains <sha>` locally, or `gh api` / `git log` for remote verification)
3. If found, check whether it is the HEAD commit of that branch
4. Print result status

### Output examples (for better description, not exactly required)

```
$ ./check-release-build ./crane --repo=migtools/crane --branch=release-0.10

Binary:   ./crane
Version:  v0.10.0
SHA:      a9de312f...
Repo:     migtools/crane
Branch:   release-0.10

✅ GREEN — SHA a9de312f is the latest commit on release-0.10
```

```
$ ./check-release-build ./crane --repo=migtools/crane --branch=release-0.10

Binary:   ./crane
Version:  v0.10.0
SHA:      8c95ff1a...
Repo:     migtools/crane
Branch:   release-0.10

⚠️  YELLOW — SHA 8c95ff1a exists on release-0.10 but is 2 commits behind HEAD (a9de312f)
```

```
$ ./check-release-build ./mta-ops --repo=migtools/mta-crane --branch=mta-8.2

Binary:   ./mta-ops
Version:  v0.10.0
SHA:      deadbeef...
Repo:     migtools/mta-crane
Branch:   mta-8.2

❌ RED — SHA deadbeef not found on branch mta-8.2
```

## Possible parameters

| Parameter    | Required | Description                                          | Example                    |
|--------------|----------|------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|
| `binary`     | yes      | Path to the built binary (positional)                | `./crane`                  |
| `--repo`     | yes      | GitHub repository (owner/name)                       | `migtools/crane`           |
| `--branch`   | yes      | Expected branch the build should come from           | `release-0.10`             |
| `--remote`   | no       | Use GitHub API instead of local git (default: false) | `--remote`                 |

## Expected branch mappings (reference)

| Binary    | Repo               | Branch         | Release         |
|-----------|--------------------| ---------------|-----------------|
| crane     | migtools/crane     | main           | nightly     |
| crane     | migtools/crane     | release-0.10   | v0.10.x         |
| `downstream-binary`   | migtools/mta-crane | mta-8.2        | `downstream name` 8.2.x       |

### Description
The `--export-dir` (or `-e`) flag is registered under the `apply` command but is completely unused. The command runs successfully even if a non-existent path is provided. 

This dead code is a leftover from when `apply` executed all stages sequentially (which was changed to only applying the final stage by default to avoid breaking changes).

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Run the `apply` command with a fake export directory:
   `./mta-ops apply -t transform -o output --export-dir /path/does/not/exist --overwrite`

### Expected Behavior
If the flag is indeed required or used, it should fail when pointing to a non-existent path. Since it is obsolete, it should be removed from the `apply` command CLI registration and relevant tests.

### Actual Behavior
The command ignores the fake path entirely and successfully generates the output:

```powershell
tdinavet@tdinavet-mac mta-ops-8.2.0-darwin-arm64 % ./mta-ops_darwin_arm64 apply -t transform -o output --export-dir /path/does/not/exist --overwrite
```

## Bug: `KUBECONFIG` with multiple files breaks `crane export` and `crane validate`

  ### Summary

  Kubernetes supports multiple kubeconfig files via the `KUBECONFIG` environment variable (colon-separated paths). This works with `kubectl` and with crane's `transform`/`apply` commands, but fails in `crane export` and `crane validate`.

  ### What happens

  ```bash
  # This is standard Kubernetes usage — works everywhere
  export KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config-cluster1:~/.kube/config-cluster2

  # kubectl works fine
  kubectl --context cluster1 get pods   ✅

  # crane export fails
  crane export --context cluster1 -n my-app
  # Error: stat /home/user/.kube/config-cluster1:/home/user/.kube/config-cluster2: no such file or directory

 ```

 Crane treats the entire colon-separated string as a single file path instead of splitting it into two files and merging them.


 ### Steps to Reproduce

  1. Set KUBECONFIG with multiple paths (standard Kubernetes practice)
  2. export KUBECONFIG=$HOME/.kube/config:$HOME/.kube/config

  ### Run crane export
  ./crane export --context src -n crane-test

  ### Expected: export succeeds (kubectl works fine with the same KUBECONFIG)
  ### Actual: Error: stat /path/a:/path/b: no such file or directory

  -> Workaround

  Merge your kubeconfig files into a single file, or avoid the KUBECONFIG env var and use the --kubeconfig flag pointing to a single file

## Description

When running `crane export` with a namespace-scoped non-admin user against an inaccessible/nonexistent namespace, the command currently:

- logs many `cannot list obj in namespace ...` errors
- writes failure artifacts under `<export-dir>/failures/`
- exports no actual resources (`<export-dir>/resources/` is empty)
- still exits with code `0`

This creates a false-success signal for users and CI pipelines, because the command appears successful even though export effectively failed.

### Example context

- Command:
  - `./crane export -n does-not-exist-xyz --context src-sajid -e exportMissingA`
- Observed:
  - repeated Forbidden/cannot-list messages
  - `resources/` empty, `failures/` populated
  - exit code `0`

## Expected behavior

If export cannot list any resource types for the target namespace (effectively all return Forbidden / inaccessible), the command should:

1. Exit with non-zero status (`exit 1`)
2. Print a clear, actionable summary error

Suggested message:

`export failed: all resource types returned Forbidden for namespace <ns> — verify the namespace exists and your user has list permissions`

## Why this matters

- Prevents false positives in automation
- Makes failure mode obvious and actionable for users
- Aligns exit code semantics with actual export outcome

## Bug: `crane export` fails for resources with long names (253 chars)
  
  ### Summary

  Kubernetes allows resource names up to 253 characters. When exporting a resource with a long name, `crane export` fails with `file name too long` because the exported filename exceeds the 255-character filesystem limit (ext4,
  APFS, HFS+). 

  ### Steps to Reproduce
  
  ```bash
  # Create a ConfigMap with max-length name (253 chars)
  LONG_NAME=$(python3 -c "print('a' * 253)")
  kubectl -n my-namespace create configmap "$LONG_NAME" --from-literal=key=value

  # Export
  crane export -n my-namespace
  # Error: open export/resources/my-namespace/ConfigMap__v1_my-namespace_aaa...aaa.yaml: file name too long
  ```

  Root Cause

  The filename pattern is Kind_group_version_namespace_name.yaml. For a 253-char resource name:
  
  ConfigMap__v1_my-namespace_   (prefix: ~27+ chars)
  aaa...aaa                     (name: 253 chars)
  .yaml                         (suffix: 5 chars)
  = ~285 chars total → exceeds 255 filesystem limit

  Current Behavior

  - Export fails with exit code 1
  - Error log dumps raw Go struct: &fs.PathError{Op:"open", Path:"...", Err:0x3f}
  - Other resources in the namespace that were already written are kept, but the export is reported as failed
  - No workaround — the resource cannot be exported

  Expected Behavior

  - Export should succeed for all valid Kubernetes resources
  - Long filenames should be truncated with a hash suffix to stay within filesystem limits while avoiding collisions
  - Example: ConfigMap__v1_my-namespace_aaaa...truncated_sha256abcdef.yaml

content.body:
## Enhancement
https://github.com/konveyor/enhancements/pull/288

## Description

### Context

Crane **`export`** is **source-only**; it cannot compare the **target** cluster. MTC/mig-controller still gives operators **early visibility** when **source** GVKs (strict **group/version** + resource) are **not** available on the **destination** the same way—**warnings**, not automatic `apiVersion` rewriting.

Per **Option A** in [doc](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FbxuNnmf3HymWamEvx_QuTjBuK9bW-5qER4XTBInuEg/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.tf3t9uiwljjz), add a **dedicated read-only command** (e.g. `crane validate`) that answers: *given this bundle of manifests, does the **target** cluster expose the same strict discovery rows we care about?*

### Goal

1. **Filesystem-first:** Walk YAML under an export (and optionally transform) directory, collect distinct **`apiVersion` + `kind`** (and namespaces from metadata), use **target** discovery to resolve/check resources, and **report** GVKs that do **not** appear on the target under **strict** same `group/version` + **resource plural** rules (MTC-like).
2. **Behavior:** **Read-only**; **warn/report** only—no silent rewrite of manifests. Define **exit codes** explicitly for human vs CI use OR Ask user and rewrite.
3. **Alignment:** Keep **preferred** export behavior as today; **validate** is the place for **target-aware** checks.

---

## Proposed changes

### CLI / UX

- New command: **`crane validate`** (name subject to maintainer agreement).
- **Minimum inputs:**
  - **`--export-dir`** (or flag name consistent with Crane) — root of YAML to scan (recursive; multi-doc YAML).
  - **Target cluster:** **`--kubeconfig`**, **`--context`** (same patterns as other Crane commands that use a cluster).
  - Optional: namespace scoping / filters (product decision).
- **Output:** Human-readable **report** (e.g. table): `apiVersion`, `kind`, namespace (if namespaced), resolved resource where possible, **OK / incompatible** + short reason.
- **Exit code policy:** Document and implement (e.g. non-zero if any incompatible GVK for CI).

### Implementation

- **Scanner:** Filesystem walk; parse YAML; extract `apiVersion`, `kind`, `metadata.namespace` (and name for context).
- **Target discovery:** client-go **discovery**, **preferred-oriented** view consistent with MTC discussion in the attached doc.
- **Strict match:** Exact **`group/version`** on target + **resource plural** present; no “pick another version on target.”
- **Cohabitating resources:** Dedupe known overlapping groups for the same logical kind (mirror mig-controller **intent**; explicit list in Crane).
- **CRDs (optional phase):** Warnings for **CRD API** / CRD-backed group skew—**detection only**.

## Acceptance Criteria

### Phase 1 (implemented in #302)
- New crane validate command accepts --input-dir (defaulting to output/, crane apply's output) plus target cluster --kubeconfig/--context.
- Scans all YAML/JSON in the directory tree using proper YAML document splitting, extracts distinct apiVersion+kind+namespace tuples, and checks each against the target's discovery API using strict group/version + kind matching.
- Always prints a human-readable table to the terminal showing each GVK as OK or Incompatible with reason and suggestion. Includes a clear PASSED/FAILED result line.
- Persists a report file to --validate-dir in JSON (default) or YAML (-o yaml) for downstream tooling.
- Writes per-resource failure artifacts as YAML files to --validate-dir/failures/ for auditability.
- Suggests alternative apiVersions when the same kind exists under a different group/version on the target.
- Exit codes are deterministic: 0 = all compatible, 1 = incompatible GVKs found or error.
- Read-only: no modifications to manifests or target cluster state. Only requires discovery API access (available to all authenticated users).
- Unit tests covering YAML scanning, GVK matching, suggestion engine, report formatting, flag validation, and argument rejection.

### Phase 2 (planned in #321 )
- New --api-resources flag accepts path to kubectl api-resources -o json output for offline validation.
- Mutually exclusive with --kubeconfig/--context.
- Uses identical matching logic, report format, and exit codes as live mode.
- Report includes mode (live/offline) and source information for traceability.
- Unit tests for JSON parsing, offline matching, and mutual exclusion.

## Context

  Follow-up to #186. Depends on #188 and #256 being completed first.

  Cluster-scoped resources (ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, CRDs, etc.)
  exported by `crane export` are currently not fully supported through the
  `transform` and `apply` stages. This issue tracks making them first-class
  citizens in the full pipeline.

  ## Goal

  Ensure cluster-scoped resources pass through `export → transform → apply`
  correctly: handled by transform plugins, rendered by kustomize, and written
  to a deterministic output layout that separates them from namespaced resources.

  ## Functional requirements

  1. Cluster-scoped resources from export must be consumed by transform — not
     skipped, misclassified, or assigned a fake namespace like `default`
  2. Transform plugins (especially `KubernetesPlugin`) must handle resources
     with empty `metadata.namespace` correctly
  3. Generated patch targets for cluster-scoped resources must omit `namespace`
  4. `crane apply` must place cluster-scoped resources under
     `output/resources/_cluster/` and namespaced resources under
     `output/resources/<namespace>/`
  5. `kubectl kustomize` must succeed on every produced stage with mixed
     namespaced + cluster-scoped inputs
  6. Whiteout and patch filtering logic must work for cluster-scoped resources
  7. Filenames and paths must be deterministic across reruns
  8. Recursive `kubectl apply -R -f output/` must work for the produced layout
  9. `crane apply` must support a `--skip-cluster-scoped` flag that excludes
     cluster-scoped resources from the rendered output (for non-admin migration
     scenarios where the user cannot apply cluster-level objects)

  ## Acceptance criteria

  - [ ] ClusterRole, ClusterRoleBinding, and CRD resources survive
        transform and appear in `output/resources/_cluster/`
  - [ ] Namespaced resources remain under `output/resources/<namespace>/`
  - [ ] `--skip-cluster-scoped` flag omits cluster-scoped resources from output
  - [ ] Patch target generation for cluster-scoped resources omits namespace
  - [ ] Recursive apply of output works for mixed namespaced + cluster-scoped cases
  - [ ] Unit tests: transform writer with cluster-scoped resources
  - [ ] Unit tests: apply split-output layout for cluster-scoped resources
  - [ ] Unit/integration test: mixed namespaced + cluster-scoped pipeline
  - [ ] E2E test: at least one scenario proving cluster-scoped dependency
        migration works end to end

content.body:
**Problem**
There are no automated tests that verify Crane correctly discovers, filters, transforms, and applies cluster-scoped resources (ClusterRoleBinding, ClusterRole, SecurityContextConstraints) related to a namespace's workloads. Manual testing has confirmed the behavior, but regressions in filtering logic or the apply path for _cluster/ resources would go undetected.

**Scope**
Tests should cover the full export -> transform -> apply pipeline, not just the export step, and should validate that the target workload actually runs with the expected permissions after apply.

**Required coverage**
ClusterRoleBinding subject patterns — all supported CRB subject types that tie a cluster-scoped binding to a namespace's workload:

ServiceAccount subject (namespace + name)
Group subject (system:serviceaccounts:namespace)
User subject (system:serviceaccount:namespace:sa)
SecurityContextConstraints binding patterns (OpenShift only):

SCC granted via users (system:serviceaccount:namespace:sa)
SCC granted via groups (system:serviceaccounts:namespace)
SCC linked through CRB roleRef (direct SCC name or system:openshift:scc:name ClusterRole)

**Export validation:**

Related cluster resources appear under _cluster/; unrelated ones do not
Namespaced resources are complete under resources/namespace/
failures/ is empty when run with sufficient credentials
Transform validation:

Both namespaced and _cluster/ resources produce transform output
Cluster-scoped references (e.g. namespace in CRB subjects, SCC users/groups) are handled appropriately through the transform step

**Apply validation:**

Namespaced and cluster-scoped resources are created on the target
Workload reaches a running/available state
ServiceAccount actually has the expected ClusterRole permissions on the target (e.g. auth can-i check)
On OpenShift: pod runs under the expected SCC

**Negative / edge cases:**

Namespace-admin credentials: export succeeds for namespaced resources; _cluster/ is empty or partial; failures/ records 403s for cluster-scoped types; transform and apply of namespaced resources still work
No cluster resources: workload with no ClusterRole/CRB/SCC produces empty _cluster/, no errors
Isolation: exporting one namespace does not pull in cluster resources belonging to other namespaces

**Platform considerations:**

CRB/ClusterRole tests (SA, Group, User subjects) should work on any Kubernetes cluster
SCC tests are OpenShift-only and should be skippable on vanilla Kubernetes


**Acceptance criteria**
Every supported CRB subject pattern and SCC binding pattern has test coverage through the full pipeline (export -> transform -> apply -> validate)
Negative cases (namespace-admin, no cluster resources, isolation) are covered
Tests are CI-compatible and clearly documented for required cluster access and OpenShift vs Kubernetes

content.body:
## Enhancement
https://github.com/konveyor/enhancements/pull/288

## Summary
Currently, `crane` uses a custom in-process JSONPatch application and generates individual `transform-*` files for each resource. This makes it difficult for users to customize or inspect the transformation logic using standard Kubernetes tools and creates "monolithic" transformations where it's hard to track which plugin changed what.

This feature proposes a shift to a **Kustomize-only workflow** with a **multi-stage pipeline**. This transition will allow users to debug transformations using standard tools like `kubectl`, view transformation steps in isolated stages (e.g., generic Kubernetes fixes vs. OpenShift-specific changes).

Existing `export`, `transform`, `apply` CLI flow will still exist, just will be extended.

---

## Description

### 1. Kustomize-Native Output Layout
Instead of a flat folder of individual JSON patches, the output will be a standard Kustomize overlay. This allows users to leverage the entire Kustomize ecosystem for validation.

**Example Directory Structure:**
```text
transform-dir/
  10_KubernetesPlugin/
    kustomization.yaml
    resources/
      deployment.yaml
      service.yaml
    patches/
      default--apps-v1--Deployment--frontend.patch.yaml
```

**Why this helps:** A user can now run `kubectl kustomize transform-dir/` to see exactly what the final manifest will look like before ever running `crane apply`.

### 2. Multi-Stage Transformation Pipeline
Transformations are broken down into stages based on plugins. Each stage consumes the output of the previous one, creating a clear "chain of custody" for manifest changes.

**Example Stage Breakdown:**
* **`10_KubernetesPlugin/`**: Handles standard API removals and generic cleanup.
* **`20_OpenShiftPlugin/`**: Handles Route and ImageStream specific injections.

**Additions to CLI Workflow:**
```bash
# Run the full transformation pipeline:
crane transform --export-dir ./export

# Inspect or run only a specific stage for debugging:
crane transform --stage 20_OpenShiftPlugin

# Apply only all stages to a cluster (using kustomize on backend):
crane apply
```

### 3. Deterministic Patching & Git-Friendliness
Patch files will use a predictable naming convention:
`<namespace>--<group>-<version>--<kind>--<name>.patch.yaml`

**Why this helps:** When running transformations multiple times or in CI/CD, the filenames remain stable. This ensures that Git diffs are clean, readable, and reflect actual logic changes rather than random file ID shifts.

---

## Proposed CLI Changes

### `crane transform`
* **`--list-stages`**: Print discovered stages and exit.
* **`--stage <dir>`**: Transform only one specific stage.
* **`--force`**: Overwrite modified stage directories (dirty check, optional).

### `crane apply`
* **Kustomize Rendering**: Refactored to render outputs exclusively via `kubectl kustomize`.
* **Stage Selection**: Support for `--stages` to apply only specific parts of the pipeline.
* **Preflight Checks**: Ensure `kubectl` is available and `kustomization.yaml` is valid.

---

## Acceptance Criteria
- [x] `crane transform` generates a valid Kustomize overlay instead of `transform-*.json` files.
- [x] **Plugin Compatibility**: Existing plugins remain compatible; Crane converts their JSONPatch output into Kustomize patches automatically.
- [x] `crane apply` uses `kubectl kustomize` for rendering.
- [x] **Stage Discovery**: Multi-stage directory structure (e.g., `10_plugin/`, `20_plugin/`) is automatically discovered and processed.
- [x] **Determinism**: Stable sort for resources and patches to ensure reproducible outputs.

---

content.body:
### Description:
When applying crane's output directory to a fresh target namespace, kubectl apply -f <output-dir>/ processes files alphabetically. This causes RoleBinding resources that reference a Role to be applied before the Role itself exists on the target, resulting in a NotFound error on the first apply.

### Steps to Reproduce:

**1. Ensure a clean environment:**

```
kubectl delete namespace role-migration --context src --ignore-not-found=true
kubectl delete namespace role-migration --context tgt --ignore-not-found=true
```

**2. Set up a fresh target namespace with non-admin access:**

```
kubectl create namespace role-migration --context tgt
kubectl create rolebinding nonadmin-ns-admin \
  --clusterrole=admin \
  --user=dev \
  -n role-migration \
  --context tgt
```

**3. Set up source namespace with a Role and RoleBinding:**
```
kubectl create namespace role-migration --context src
kubectl create serviceaccount test-sa -n role-migration --context src
kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n role-migration --context src
kubectl create rolebinding pod-reader-binding --role=pod-reader --serviceaccount=role-migration:test-sa -n role-migration --context src
```

**4. Run the crane pipeline:**

```
EXPORT_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
TRANSFORM_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
OUTPUT_DIR=$(mktemp -d)

crane export --namespace role-migration --context src --export-dir "$EXPORT_DIR"
crane transform --export-dir "$EXPORT_DIR" --transform-dir "$TRANSFORM_DIR"
crane apply --export-dir "$EXPORT_DIR" --transform-dir "$TRANSFORM_DIR" --output-dir "$OUTPUT_DIR"
```

**5. Apply the output to the fresh target namespace in a single pass:**

```
KUBECONFIG=~/.kube/config \
kubectl apply \
  -f "$OUTPUT_DIR/resources/role-migration/" \
  --context tgt-dev
```

### Actual Result:
```
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/nonadmin-ns-admin configured
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader created
serviceaccount/test-sa created
Error from server (NotFound): error when creating "...RoleBinding_rbac.authorization.k8s.io_v1_role-migration_pod-reader-binding.yaml": rolebindings.rbac.authorization.k8s.io "pod-reader" not found
```

### Expected Result:
```
All resources apply successfully in a single pass.
Root Cause:
kubectl apply -f <dir> processes files alphabetically. RoleBinding sorts before Role, so pod-reader-binding is attempted before pod-reader exists on the target. Kubernetes validates the roleRef at creation time and rejects the binding.
```

### Workaround:
Run kubectl apply again, the second pass succeeds because all dependencies are already in place:

`kubectl apply -f "$OUTPUT_DIR/resources/role-migration/" --context tgt`

### Suggested Fix:
crane should write manifests to the output directory in dependency-aware order, ensuring that Role resources are written before RoleBinding resources, ConfigMap/Secret before Deployment, etc.


### Environment:
 
crane version: v0.0.6
crane-lib version: v0.0.10
Kubernetes: minikube v1.35.1
kubectl: v1.33.3

content.body:
## Description

When migrating applications from one OpenShift cluster to another using crane, the export phase captures OpenShift auto-injected namespace resources that cause `kubectl apply` failures with annotation warnings.

These issues occur **regardless of whether export/apply is done as cluster-admin or non-admin**, because OpenShift automatically injects these resources into every namespace.

## OpenShift Auto-Injected Resources

OpenShift automatically creates the following resources in every namespace:

1. **ConfigMap**: `openshift-service-ca.crt` (injected by service-ca-operator)
2. **RoleBindings**:
   - `system:deployers` (created by namespace controller)
   - `system:image-builders`
   - `system:image-pullers`
3. **ServiceAccounts**:
   - `builder`
   - `deployer`

## Current Behavior

When crane exports a namespace, it captures all resources including these auto-injected ones. When applying to the target cluster, `kubectl apply` generates warnings:

```
Warning: resource configmaps/openshift-service-ca.crt is missing the
kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation which is
required by kubectl apply. kubectl apply should only be used on resources
created declaratively by either kubectl create --save-config or kubectl apply.
The missing annotation will be patched automatically.

Warning: resource rolebindings/system:deployers is missing the
kubectl.kubernetes.io/last-applied-configuration annotation...
Warning: resource rolebindings/system:image-builders is missing...

Warning: resource rolebindings/system:image-pullers is missing...

Warning: resource serviceaccounts/builder is missing...

Warning: resource serviceaccounts/deployer is missing...
```
Depending on kubectl version and flags, these warnings may cause the apply to fail with exit code 1.

## Expected Behavior

The `crane-plugin-openshift` plugin should filter these resources during the **transform** phase

content.body:
## Summary
`crane export` captures the `openshift-service-ca.crt` ConfigMap and 
OpenShiftPlugin does not filter it out during transform. This ConfigMap 
is OCP-managed, auto-created and populated by the `service-ca` operator 
in every namespace. it is never created by the user.

## Expected Behavior
`openshift-service-ca.crt` should be filtered out by OpenShiftPlugin 
since it is OCP-specific, cluster-specific, and automatically recreated 
by the target cluster's `service-ca` operator. This is analogous to how 
KubernetesPlugin filters `kube-root-ca.crt`.

## Actual Behavior
`openshift-service-ca.crt` passes through transform and appears in the 
final output manifest, ready to be applied to the target cluster.

## Risk
- The cert data is injected at runtime via annotation 
  (`service.beta.openshift.io/inject-cabundle`), so in most cases the 
  exported ConfigMap is empty and applying it is harmless today
- However if the ConfigMap carries data, applying it to the target would 
  overwrite the target cluster's own service CA cert in that namespace, 
  potentially breaking TLS for any workload relying on it for internal 
  service communication

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Create a namespace on an OCP source cluster
2. Run `crane export`
3. Run `crane transform` (without OpenShiftPlugin stage — KubernetesPlugin only)
4. Check output: `openshift-service-ca.crt` ConfigMap is present

## Proposed Fix
Add `openshift-service-ca.crt` to the OpenShiftPlugin filter list.

Notes on possible solution: https://github.com/aufi/move-crane/blob/main/drafts/STAGE_DIRECTORY_REFACTOR_PLAN.md Not sure if this can address all the complexity, but it should help (and should be quite safe to implement now). ## Other options Anything else was proposed from engineering team. In order to fit them to existing transform stages, it looked good to me to have them in a separate directory to differentiate what resources are processed (got as an input for given stage) and what are created as new by the given stage (typically by a plugin in BuildConfig->ShipWright or DeploymentConfig scenarios).
```
# manually installed OpenShift and ImageStream plugins as addition to KubernetesPlugin to see maximum of possible optional flags
$ crane transform optionals
Plugin: KubernetesPlugin (version v0.0.10)
    add-annotations: Annotations to add to each resource
        Example: annotation1=value1,annotation2=value2
    registry-replacement: Map of image registry paths to swap on transform, in the format original-registry1=target-registry1,original-registry2=target-registry2...
        Example: docker-registry.default.svc:5000=image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000,docker.io/foo=quay.io/bar
    remove-annotations: Annotations to remove
        Example: annotation1,annotation2
    disable-whiteout-owned: Disable whiting out owned pods and pod template resources
        Example: true
    extra-whiteouts: Additional resources to whiteout specified as a comma-separated list of GroupKind strings.
        Example: Deployment.apps,Service,Route.route.openshift.io
    include-only: If specified, every resource not listed here will be a whiteout. extra-whiteouts is ignored when include-only is specified. Specified as a comma-separated list of GroupKind strings.
        Example: Deployment.apps,Service,Route.route.openshift.io
    strip-default-rbac: Whether to strip default RBAC including default serviceAccount (default: true)
        Example: true
    strip-default-cabundle: Whether to strip default CA Bundle (default: true)
        Example: true
    pvc-rename-map: A comma-separated list of colon separated pvc renames.
        Example: old-pvc1-name:new-pvc1-name,old-pvc2-name:new-pvc2-name
Plugin: ImagestreamPlugin (version v0.0.2)
    src-internal-registry: Internal registry hostname[:port] used to determine whether an istag references a local image
        Example: image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000
Plugin: OpenShiftPlugin (version v0.0.4)
    strip-default-rbac: Whether to strip default RBAC including builder and deployers serviceAccounts, roleBindings for admin, builders, and deployers (default: true)
        Example: true
    strip-default-cabundle: Whether to strip default CA Bundle (default: true)
        Example: true
    strip-default-pull-secrets: Whether to strip Pod and BuildConfig default pull secrets (beginning with builder/default/deployer-dockercfg-) that aren't replaced by the map param pull-secret-replacement (default: true)
        Example: true
    pull-secret-replacement: Map of pull secrets to replace in Pods and BuildConfigs while transforming in format secret1=destsecret1,secret2=destsecret2[...]
        Example: default-dockercfg-h4n7g=default-dockercfg-12345,builder-dockercfg-abcde=builder-dockercfg-12345
    registry-replacement: Map of image registry paths to swap on transform, in the format original-registry1=target-registry1,original-registry2=target-registry2...
        Example: docker-registry.default.svc:5000=image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000,docker.io/foo=quay.io/bar
    pvc-rename-map: A comma-separated list of colon separated pvc renames.
        Example: old-pvc1-name:new-pvc1-name,old-pvc2-name:new-pvc2-name
```

This was not yet re-considered how this should look like in multistage transformation. Probably the main question I think needs to answered is if the KubernetesPlugin with default options together with possibility have custom stages (based on kustomize) can  provide the same or more features than optional flags for legacy plugins. Or if there could be good use-case for other plugins (e.g. like passing fragment of kustomization together with a custom stage creation).

In the end, this could be a bug either
- there is an `optionals` CLI arg, that is redundant/misleading/.. and should be removed
- there is an `optionals` CLI arg, that needs to be fixed to correctly work with multistage transformation (update multistage transform (and instructions file) to allow passing these options for each stage (it can be different for each stage))

content.body:
## Standalone Jobs re-execute on target cluster after migration

  ### Summary

  When migrating standalone Jobs (not created by CronJobs) through the crane pipeline (export → transform → apply), they re-execute on the target cluster regardless of whether they already completed on the source. There is no mechanism to prevent this.

  ### Why This Matters

  - Some Jobs are **app-critical init Jobs** (e.g., MTA Hub database setup, WordPress site initialization). These are idempotent and safe to re-run. Whiteout-ing them would break the app on the target since the Deployment
  depends on the Job having run first.
  - Some Jobs are **historical one-shot Jobs** (e.g., a data import that already completed). Re-running these could be harmful or wasteful.
  - Crane cannot distinguish between these two types as both are standalone Jobs with no ownerReferences.

  ### Current Behavior

  | Job Type | Exported? | Whiteout-ed? | Applied to Target? | Re-runs? |
  |----------|-----------|-------------|--------------------|---------|
  | CronJob | Yes | No | Yes | Preserves source suspend state (correct) |
  | CronJob-spawned Job | Yes | Yes (ownerRef) | No | N/A (correct) |
  | Standalone Job | Yes | No | Yes (after PR #138) | Yes, always |

  ### Options

  **If we whiteout standalone Jobs:**
  - Historical one-shot Jobs won't re-run (good)
  - But app-critical init Jobs (MTA Hub db-setup, WordPress install) are silently dropped — app breaks on target because its initialization never runs

  **If we suspend standalone Jobs (`spec.suspend: true`):**
  - Job definition exists on target but doesn't auto-execute
  - User must manually unsuspend each Job — extra step that could be forgotten
  - Init Jobs that need to run before the app starts would require the user to know the correct ordering (unsuspend Job first, then wait for completion, then deploy the app — but in crane's output everything is in one YAML)

content.body:
The crane CLI tool migrates kubernetes resources (YAML manifests) and could migrate volume data using migrate-pvc, however it cannot migrate Images between cluster images registries (this is a use-case for tools like https://github.com/podman-container-tools/skopeo).

This issue primary focuses on internal image registries like it was common in OpenShift use-cases. Images from  outside of the cluster registries like quay.io, ghcr.io, etc. are not affected, since they could be pulled by the source&target cluster.

## Solution 1: Document internal images usage

Internal image registry is common in OpenShift clusters (unlike to upstream k8s cluster). This registry usage could be visible in exported data in a CR `Group: "image.openshift.io", Kind: "ImageStream"`, if this is present in exported manifests, crane should inform user, that referenced images are NOT migrated automatically and provide a doc how to migrate images outside of the crane.

This information form is TBD (logging, adding some report or warning?) need to clarify what fits well to crane CLI migration flow.

## Possible solution 2: Migrate images directly (unconfirmed, maybe later)

Help crane user migrate those images by either generating commands to migrate images using external tool like `skopeo` (example https://github.com/migtools/crane/blob/main/cmd/skopeo-sync-gen/skopeo-sync-gen.go) or run the images migration on behalf of user in orchestrated or UI-triggered migration workflows once they are implemented. Implementation of this solution is not planned at this moment.

content.body:
## Feature Request

The `plugin-manager` should provide an `info` subcommand that gives users more information about the specified plugin.

## Description

Currently, the plugin-manager subcommand supports listing of the available plugins, for example:

```
$ crane plugin-manager list --params
Listing from the repo default
+-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|    NAME     |  SHORTDESCRIPTION  |        DESCRIPTION         | AVAILABLEVERSIONS |                                                                                   OPTIONALFIELDS                                                                                   |
+-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| pvc         | pvc                | this is pvc                | 0.0.1             |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
+-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| hc-whiteout | hc-whiteout plugin | this is hc-whiteout plugin | 0.0.1             |                                                                                                                                                                                    |
+-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| openshift   | openshift          | this is openshift          | 1.0.7             | - FlagName: StripDefaultPullSecrets                                                                                                                                                |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Help: Whether to strip Pod and BuildConfig default pull secrets (beginning with builder/default/deployer-dockercfg-) that aren't replaced by the map param PullSecretReplacement |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Example: true                                                                                                                                                                    |
|             |                    |                            |                   | - FlagName: PullSecretReplacement                                                                                                                                                  |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Help: Map of pull secrets to replace in Pods and BuildConfigs while transforming in format secret1=destsecret1,secret2=destsecret2[...]                                          |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Example: default-dockercfg-h4n7g=default-dockercfg-12345,builder-dockercfg-abcde=builder-dockercfg-12345                                                                         |
|             |                    |                            |                   | - FlagName: RegistryReplacement                                                                                                                                                    |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Help: Map of image registry paths to swap on transform, in the format original-registry1=target-registry1,original-registry2=target-registry2...                                 |
|             |                    |                            |                   |   Example: docker-registry.default.svc:5000=image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000,docker.io/foo=quay.io/bar                                                             |
+-------------+--------------------+----------------------------+-------------------+------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

```

However, this doesn't give the end user much insight into what the plugin does, how it does it, or the when/why the end user would install and use it.
 
And instead of using table to consume this information, output similar to something like following makes more sense:

```
Name:                  OpenshiftPlugin
ShortDescription:    <short-description>
Description:            <description>
Version:                   <version>
OptionalFields:        <optional-fields>
```
 
## Solution

Introduce an `info` subcommand that provides long form explanation of a specified user plugin.

## Alternative Solutions

* Populating the `SHORTDESCRIPTION` and `DESCRIPTION` with an actual description :sunglasses: might lessen the need for a new `info` command.
* Change the output from table to similar to something that is mentioned above.

content.body:
**What is your persona?**

I'm an application developer that is designing a POC of an open-source application that integrates crane to export the configuration of an application.

**What is your story / use case?**

As a user of the `crane export` command, I want to include all the non-namespaced (e.g. cluster scoped) RBAC resources that are linked to the `ServiceAccount` defined in the exported namespace(s), so that the generated manifests can be deployed on a new environment with no further manual operations.

Using an optional flag to the `crane export` command, like `--cluster-scoped-rbac` (defaulted to "false" to disable the requested feature), at the end of the crane export-transform-apply pipeline, we can generate a complete and consistent set of manifests that can be deployed on any environment without any manual intervention to setup the RBAC aspects.

**Do you have a suggestion for implementation?**

I would implement this as an optional flag in the crane core module, since the export command does not support the concept of plugin. 

Since we want only some of these cluster-scoped resources, we should define somewhere the list of managed types (e.g., `ClusterRole`, `ClusterRoleBinding` and, in case of OpenShift cluster, also `SecurityContextConstraints`) and load them only after all the configured namespaces have been exported, to discard those that are not connected to any of the exported `ServiceAccount` (maybe a cache can be required to store all of them, or at least their namespace and name pairs).

Once selected, those manifests can be stored in a dedicated folder, with a name that can't match a namespace name, like `_cluster`.

While the contributors review the issue, I would start developing the feature to validate the proposed solution.

**What is your persona?**

I'm a cluster administrator for several clusters with a high level of privilege. I need to export, clean and re-deploy applications between stages/clusters quite regularly.

**What is your story / use case?**

As an administrator, I want to be able to specify additional JSONPatch operations, so that I can remove additional cluster/Rancher-specific fields from the transformed manifests.

We use Rancher to manage our K8S Clusters, and Rancher has its own set of annotations that are sometimes embedded in .spec.template.metadata.annotations. I need to remove these fields to get a clean manifest for re-deployment in another cluster.

We often have developers build an application or middleware deployment in a testing cluster, and we need to export the manifests, clean them, and create modules for later reuse.

If JSONPatch tests could be used to skip execution on a per-manifest basis (instead of the whole crane apply operation), that would be welcome.

**Do you have a suggestion for implementation?**

An additional flag for `crane transform` that points to a file/directory containing JSONPatch operations.

content.body:
In order to reach feature parity with MTC, we need have the export action covering cluster-level resources, that are referenced from the workloads that is being migrated. Examples are custom SCC (security contexts), ServiceAccount (relying on ClusterRoleBinding) or RoleAggregation.

Crane export action currently uses velero discovery library (https://github.com/migtools/crane/blob/main/cmd/export/export.go#L12-L14). In order to have full control over this logic now and also in future, it is needed re-consired if this library is needed and it make sense continue using it, or we want implement own code that would be resposible for this functionality. In such case, the code needs to be implemented and velero discovery dependency removed from crane. This is the first part of the task.

If the migrated workload uses some of custom cluster-level resources in its manifest, it is expected they don't exist in target cluster, so they need to be created during migration. This task covers only export part of required cluster-level resources. So it is needed update export to gather those resources (typically from different namespaces) along with currently exported manifests.

Ability to export cluster-level resources required login with cluster-admin permissions, crane should try export all referenced cluster-level resources by default, if such resources exist and the export failed for lack of permission, export action should warn user about it (but allow finish export without it).

The task output should be PR(s) in crane repo updating `export` action as described above.

Validate the crane OCP image migration workflow for images that were pushed 
directly to the internal registry without a BuildConfig.

Unlike S2I/BuildConfig-based images, there is no rebuild safety net on the 
destination, skopeo is the only migration path.

   source internal registry (no BuildConfig involved)

4) Deploy an app (Deployment + Service) referencing that ImageStream

7) crane skopeo-sync-gen -- verify the manually-pushed image is detected
8) crane transform (KubernetesPlugin + OpenShiftPlugin stages)
9) crane apply
10) skopeo copy the exact digest from source to destination registry
11) kubectl apply -f output/resources/<ns>/
12) Verify on destination: Deployment pulls correct image, no ErrImagePull,
    ImageStreamTag points to same digest as source

**Pass Criteria:**
- skopeo-sync-gen detects the manually-pushed image 
- ImageStreamTag on destination matches source digest 
- Deployment pulls successfully without ErrImagePull

content.body:
Subscription (and potentially other OLM/operator resources like ClusterServiceVersion) are currently not part of the transform whiteout/skip list.
As a result, when these resources are discovered during export, they are carried through transform and remain in the final output directory generated by crane apply.

This is different from resources like Endpoints, which are explicitly whiteouted in transform and therefore skipped from final output.

Why this is a problem
For ignored-resource scenarios (e.g. MTC-127), operator-managed resources are expected to be excluded from final migration manifests. Current behavior includes them, which leads to unexpected output and test failures.

Expected behavior
If operator resources are meant to be ignored by default, transform should explicitly whiteout/skip them (similar to Endpoints) so they do not appear in final output.

Actual behavior
Subscription manifests appear in final output after running the pipeline (export -> transform -> apply), because no transform whiteout rule currently removes them.

content.body:
## Enhancement
https://github.com/konveyor/enhancements/pull/288

## Story

Namespaces often hold workloads that **depend on cluster-scoped objects** (RBAC, OpenShift SCCs, aggregations, CRDs for custom types, etc.). Those objects may be **missing on the target cluster** but are required for the app to run. This epic extends Crane toward **MTC-style behavior**: discover and export **referenced cluster-level dependencies**, then **transform and apply** them, with a clear story for **escalated permissions** (e.g. cluster-admin) when namespace admins cannot create cluster-scoped resources.


## Subtasks

| Issue | Title |
|-------|--------|
| #184 | Explore and document MTC logic for migrating cluster level resources |
| #186 | Update export action with cluster-level dependencies |
| #189 | Update transform & apply for cluster-level resources |

- **#184** — Discovery / design input: how MTC finds and migrates linked cluster resources; guidelines for Crane. *(Closed when doc/deliverable is done.)*
- **#186** — **Export:** extend `crane export` to gather referenced cluster-level resources; document behavior when the user lacks permissions (warn, still finish export where possible). Export-only scope; consider Velero discovery vs owned discovery per issue text.
- **#189** — **Transform & apply:** handle exported cluster-scoped manifests in the pipeline. Issue text references **#188** as a prerequisite (confirm scope there).

## Proposed changes

1. **Documented parity baseline (#184)** — Agreed write-up of which cluster-level types MTC considers, how they are tied to a namespace migration, and when elevated permissions are needed.
2. **Export (#186)** — Emit referenced cluster-level dependencies alongside namespace workloads; default to attempting export; on forbidden/partial failure, warn and allow export to complete with partial data where applicable.
3. **Transform & apply (#189)** — Support new/changed export layout and kinds through transform and apply (flags, ordering, docs as needed), aligned with **#188** as applicable.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] mig-controller parity baseline from #184 is available and reviewed as the design input for Crane behavior.
- [ ]  crane export covers referenced cluster-scoped dependencies with documented permission-denied behavior (#186).
- [ ]  crane transform and crane apply support exported cluster-scoped artifacts without breaking existing namespace-only workflows (#189).
- [ ]  Apply ordering is correct: CRDs → cluster RBAC/security → namespace resources.
- [ ]  Scope-filtering flags (--cluster-scoped-only, --namespace-scoped-only) enable split-responsibility workflows between namespace admins and cluster admins.
- [ ] User-facing documentation covers permissions requirements, default behavior, relevant flags, and apply ordering.
- [ ]  E2E test covering export → transform → apply with at least one cluster-scoped dependency and one partial-export path when cluster-level access is forbidden.
- [ ]  #188 dependency for #189 is resolved or explicitly folded into #189 scope.

content.body:
## Description

When migrating a stateful application (MongoDB) using crane transfer-pvc, directories on the source PVC owned by an application-specific uid (e.g. uid 999, the mongodb user) with 700 permissions are silently skipped by rsync. The destination pod starts with an empty database, with no clear indication to the user that data was not transferred.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Deploy MongoDB on source cluster via k8s-apps-deployer (or any deployment that runs MongoDB as uid 999)
2. Insert test documents into the database
3. Run crane transfer-pvc without any pre-steps
4. Deploy MongoDB on dest cluster using the transferred PVC
5. Query the database — collection is empty (count: 0)

## Actual behavior

```
Status: Partially failed
Failed files:
  - /mnt/mongo/data/.mongodb [Permission denied (13)]
  - /mnt/mongo/data/_tmp [Permission denied (13)]
  - /mnt/mongo/data/diagnostic.data [Permission denied (13)]
  - /mnt/mongo/data/journal [Permission denied (13)]
```
## Expected behavior

All files on the source PVC are transferred regardless of file ownership. The destination database contains all source data. This is how MTC/Velero handles the same scenario, velero runs with elevated privileges and reads all files regardless of ownership without any user intervention.

## Root cause

The rsync-server and rsync-client pods spawned by crane transfer-pvc run as uid 1000. MongoDB writes its data directories (journal/, _tmp/, diagnostic.data/, .mongodb/) as uid 999 with 700 (owner-only) permissions. rsync running as uid 1000 cannot read these directories and skips them silently.

## Workaround

```
# Run as root on source PVC before transfer-pvc
chmod -R 755 <source-pvc-mount>
```

content.body:
## Summary

- **Problem:** `crane export` can fail with **`no such file or directory`** when writing a **`CustomResourceDefinition`** under `resources/<namespace>/_cluster/`.
- **Cause:** `_cluster` is only created when an earlier step decides cluster-scoped manifests exist. **CRDs are added later** in the same run but still write to `_cluster`, so the directory may **never be created**.
- **Impact:** Valid namespaces that only trigger CRD export (no other `_cluster` content) can **fail the whole export**.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Create namespace, CRD, and CR:

```bash
export CTX=<your-context>
export NS=crane-exp-crd-repro

kubectl create namespace "$NS" --context "$CTX" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply --context "$CTX" -f -

kubectl apply --context "$CTX" -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: widgets.craneexplore.test
spec:
  group: craneexplore.test
  scope: Namespaced
  names:
    plural: widgets
    singular: widget
    kind: Widget
  versions:
    - name: v1
      served: true
      storage: true
      schema:
        openAPIV3Schema:
          type: object
          properties:
            spec:
              type: object
              properties:
                note:
                  type: string
EOF

kubectl apply --context "$CTX" -n "$NS" -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: craneexplore.test/v1
kind: Widget
metadata:
  name: widget-one
spec:
  note: "repro"
EOF
```

2. Export to a clean directory:

```bash
rm -rf ./exp-repro && mkdir ./exp-repro
crane export -e ./exp-repro --namespace "$NS" --context "$CTX"
```

## Actual behavior

| Item | Detail |
|------|--------|
| **Logs** | Indicate `_cluster` is empty / not needed for the initial cluster-scoped pass |
| **Failure** | Open `.../resources/<namespace>/_cluster/CustomResourceDefinition_*.yaml` fails (**parent dir missing**) |
| **Exit** | Non-zero |

## Expected behavior

- **`_cluster`** exists **before** any write to `.../_cluster/*.yaml`,
so this scenario completes **without** a missing-directory error.

## Environment

- **Crane:** `main` 
- **Cluster:** e.g. minikube (not cloud-specific)
